title: How do you create brainstorming buckets quickly when your mind goes blank?
description: Simple splits for brainstorming for case interviews. When you need buckets fast for "What else could they do?" A checklist, a worked example and how to say…
hook: When an interviewer asks for ideas and your mind goes blank, a simple split can rescue you. These pairs give you instant buckets for almost any brainstorm.
body:
When it helps

When you need buckets fast for "What else could they do?"

The splits

  • Internal vs external
  • Short term vs long term
  • Revenue vs costs
  • Supply vs demand
  • Quantitative vs qualitative
  • Pros vs cons
  • Organic vs inorganic
  • Direct vs indirect
  • Financial vs non-financial

An example

"How could a museum increase visitor numbers?" Pick a split: internal versus external. Internal: new exhibitions, longer opening hours, a better café, easier online booking. External: partnerships with schools, tourism boards, hotels, events in the city. In ten seconds you have two clean buckets, and you look organised even though you had no time to prepare.

How it sounds in an interview

Let me split this into what the client can change itself, and what involves outside partners. On the internal side...

A practical escape when the case feels blank

Imagine the interviewer asks why a bicycle-sharing service's revenue fell. Start with a split that creates measurable branches: rides × average revenue per ride. If rides are down, split further into active riders × rides per rider. If revenue per ride is down, examine base fare, ride duration, discounts and user mix.

You can also split by time (weekday/weekend), place (central/suburban), customer (commuters/tourists) and channel (app/partner). Choose the split most likely to explain the problem, not all four just to sound comprehensive.

Suppose the total is down 12%, but weekend rides are stable while weekday commuting rides are down 30%. You have narrowed the investigation: look at commuting patterns, station availability and price changes on weekday routes. A strong structure earns its keep by directing the next analysis, not by filling a page with boxes.
